title: Adverbs: How Things Happen
summary: Use adverbs to say how actions happen. Form common -ly adverbs, recognise words that do not change, and distinguish good from well.
learningObjectives: Form regular -ly adverbs from adjectives, including easy and heavy.
Choose an adverb rather than an adjective to describe how an action happens.
Use hard, fast, late and early as adverbs without adding -ly.
Choose good for a description and well for performing an action.
Recognise well as an adjective when talking about health.

explanation.heading: An adverb tells us how an action happens
explanation.body: Use an adverb when you want to describe how somebody does something or how something happens. Many adverbs of manner end in -ly: move slowly, speak clearly or close a door carefully.
explanation.example: The children listened quietly to the story.

explanation.heading: Form many adverbs with -ly
explanation.body: Many adjectives become adverbs by adding -ly: calm → calmly and polite → politely. With an adjective ending in consonant + y, change y to i before -ly: easy → easily and heavy → heavily.
explanation.example: The rain fell heavily during the night.

explanation.heading: Adjective or adverb?
explanation.body: Use an adjective to describe a person or thing, often after be or feel: he was nervous. Use an adverb to describe the action: he spoke nervously. Do not automatically add -ly after look, feel, sound, smell or taste when these verbs describe their subject.
explanation.example: The dancer was graceful and moved gracefully.

explanation.heading: Hard, fast, late and early do not need -ly
explanation.body: Some words have the same form as an adjective and an adverb. Say work hard, run fast, arrive late and get up early. Hardly does not mean hard: it usually means almost not.
explanation.example: The baker starts early and works hard.

explanation.heading: Good, well and health
explanation.body: Good is an adjective; well is normally the corresponding adverb. Say a good singer but sing well. Well can also be an adjective meaning healthy: I am well today.
explanation.example: The chef is good at her job and cooks well.

comparisons.title: Describe the person or the action

right.label: Adverb
right.note: Carefully describes how the driver turned.

right.label: Well = adverb
right.note: Well describes how the actors performed.

examples.sentence: The nurse explained the instructions clearly.
examples.note: Clearly describes how the nurse explained something.

examples.sentence: My little sister learns new games easily.
examples.note: Easy changes to easily when it is an adverb.

examples.sentence: The cyclist rode fast along the empty road.
examples.note: Fast has the same form as an adjective and an adverb.

examples.sentence: We worked hard to finish the garden before dark.
examples.note: Hard is the correct adverb; hardly has a different meaning.

examples.sentence: I was ill last week, but I am well now.
examples.note: Well can mean healthy when it follows am.

commonMistakes.why: Carefully is an adverb describing the action of reading.
The adverb from easy is easily.
Well, not good, describes how someone speaks.
Hard means with effort; hardly means almost not.

studyTips: Ask what the word describes: a person or thing usually needs an adjective; an action usually needs an adverb.
Practise spelling: easy → easily, heavy → heavily, careful → carefully.
Remember the short set of adverbs with no -ly: work hard, run fast, arrive late and wake up early.

exercises.prompt: Choose the word that completes the sentence: Please check the address ___ before you leave.
exercises.feedback: Carefully is an adverb describing how to check the address.

exercises.prompt: Choose the word that completes the sentence: Theo rides his bicycle ___.
exercises.feedback: Fast is already an adverb; fastly is not used here.

exercises.prompt: Choose the word that completes the sentence: The musicians played ___ at the festival.
exercises.feedback: Well is the adverb that describes how the musicians played.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct word: We arrived ___ for the first train.
exercises.feedback: Early works as an adverb without an -ly ending.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the adverb from 'easy': The children solved the puzzle ___.
exercises.feedback: Easy changes to easily when it describes how an action happens.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the adverb from 'heavy': Rain fell ___ during the storm.
exercises.feedback: The adverb from heavy changes y to i before -ly.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the adverb from 'bad': The old radio worked ___ yesterday.
exercises.feedback: Badly is the adverb from bad, describing how the radio worked.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the correct adverb from 'hard': At the bakery, Maya works ___ all morning.
exercises.feedback: Hard is the adverb of effort; hardly would change the meaning.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Please speak slow so everyone can understand.
acceptedAnswers: Please speak slowly so everyone can understand.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The waiter carried the glasses very careful.
acceptedAnswers: The waiter carried the glasses very carefully.
exercises.feedback: Carefully is the adverb that modifies carried.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: My brother can swim fastly.
exercises.feedback: Fast is already an adverb; do not add -ly.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The singer performed good at the concert.
acceptedAnswers: The singer performed well at the concert.
exercises.feedback: Well is the adverb for how someone performed.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the complete sentence using the adverb 'neatly': 'Mina writes ___.'
speakingExercises.feedback: Neatly is the adverb describing how Mina writes.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct this sentence aloud: 'My uncle drives fastly.'
speakingExercises.feedback: Fast already has the correct adverb form.

speakingExercises.prompt: Complete the sentence aloud using 'well': 'Dalia plays the piano ___.'
speakingExercises.feedback: Well describes how Dalia plays the piano.

speakingExercises.prompt: The guide explained the route in a clear way. Say the complete sentence beginning 'The guide explained the route' and ending with the adverb from 'clear'.
acceptedAnswers: The guide explained the route clearly.
speakingExercises.feedback: Clearly is the adverb from clear. It describes how the guide explained the route.

speakingExercises.prompt: Change 'Sara is a careful driver' to a sentence beginning 'Sara drives' and using the adverb from 'careful'.
speakingExercises.feedback: Careful describes a driver; carefully describes how Sara drives.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend asks how the children learned the dance. They learned it without difficulty. Begin 'The children learned the dance' and end with the adverb from 'easy'.
acceptedAnswers: The children learned the dance easily.
speakingExercises.feedback: Easy changes to easily: y becomes i before -ly.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend means that Leo puts in a lot of effort, but says 'Leo studies hardly every evening.' Correct the sentence, keeping 'Leo studies' and 'every evening'.
speakingExercises.feedback: Hard means with effort; hardly means almost not. Hard is correct for studying with effort.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe this bus trip in exactly two sentences: the driver drove slowly because the road was wet, and all passengers arrived safely. Begin with 'The driver', then 'All passengers'.
acceptedAnswers: The driver drove slowly because the road was wet. All passengers arrived safely.
speakingExercises.feedback: Slowly tells how the driver drove, and safely tells how the passengers arrived.

listeningExercises.audioText: The guests walked quietly into the library.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which word tells you how the guests walked?
listeningExercises.feedback: Quietly is the adverb you hear describing how the guests walked.

listeningExercises.audioText: I got up early to catch the bus.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which adverb do you hear telling you when the speaker got up?
listeningExercises.feedback: Early is the adverb heard in the sentence; no -ly is added.

listeningExercises.audioText: She answered the difficult question correctly.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the adverb that describes how she answered.
listeningExercises.feedback: Correctly describes the way she answered the question.

listeningExercises.audioText: The shop assistant replied politely when the customer asked for help.
listeningExercises.prompt: How did the assistant treat the customer?
listeningExercises.feedback: Politely means with good manners; it describes the way the assistant replied.

listeningExercises.audioText: Omar arrived late at the station, so he missed the first train.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why did Omar miss the train?
choices: He arrived after it had gone.
He chose to stay at home.
listeningExercises.feedback: Omar missed the first train because he arrived late, after it had left.

listeningExercises.audioText: The soup tastes good, and the chef always cooks well.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker say about the chef?
choices: The chef prepares food too slowly.
listeningExercises.feedback: Cooks well means prepares food skilfully. Good describes the soup; well describes the cooking.

listeningExercises.audioText: The rain fell heavily during the storm last night.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the adverb you hear that describes how the rain fell.
listeningExercises.feedback: Heavily is the adverb formed from heavy by changing y to i before -ly.

listeningExercises.audioText: The students worked hard on the final exercise.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the adverb you hear immediately after 'worked'.
listeningExercises.feedback: Hard describes working with effort. Hardly would mean almost not, which changes the meaning.
